extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of The Spectator / readers interested in manners, morals, and natural philosophy (early-18th-century English audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing short moral and observational essays on manners, rural life, natural philosophy, and social conduct — showing how to ground reflections in anecdote and concrete detail. Emphasises tone, moderation, and the use of examples to argue philosophical points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hunting as wholesome exercise (moderation & motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hunting is laudable when it is 'The Preservation of Health, and keeping all the Organs of the Soul in a Condition to execute her Orders' rather than merely to 'drown Thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribe the moderate use of hunting (author intends to hunt twice a week) as 'the best kind of Physick' for mending or preserving constitution; contrast legitimate healthful exercise with excessive pastime pursued to avoid self-reflection (Pascal's criticism). Example quotation and Dryden lines are offered to support hunting-as-exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess motive behind pastimes
rubrics_metrics.description: One should judge sports and amusements by their motive: whether they preserve health and faculties or serve merely to 'drown Thought' and avoid introspection (Pascal's point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a pastime, ask whether the participant pursues it for laudable ends (health, moderation) or to evade self-examination. The text contrasts moderate, healthful exercise with obsessive devotion to sport that consumes the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and report concrete discipline in scenes (use specific, observable detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe observable particulars of a scene (e.g. 'Deference which the rest of the Pack paid to each particular Hound...If they were at Fault, and an old Hound of Reputation opened but once, he was immediately followed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, precise detail about behaviour and hierarchy (how hounds follow reputed leaders, obedience to a pole signal) to make a scene lively and informative. Such particulars support broader reflections and moral lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical neutrality on extraordinary claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When arguments press equally on both sides, 'the safest Method is to give up our selves to neither' — adopt a hovering or neutral faith rather than decisive assent to extraordinary reports (e.g. witchcraft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspend belief on particular extraordinary instances until sufficiently certain accounts are provided. The author models believing generally in a phenomenon yet refusing credit to specific, unverified stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish general hypothesis from unverified particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: I believe in general that there is such a thing as Witch-craft, 'but at the same time can give no Credit to any particular Instance of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a distinction between accepting a general possibility and accepting testimony of individual cases — require corroboration before accepting specific allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing malice to infirmity; preserve compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities often turn 'an old Woman' into a witch when she grows chargeable to the parish; this 'cuts off Charity' and inspires malevolence toward the infirm and doting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In both moral judgment and narrative portrayal, beware of conflating age/infirmity with culpability. Show compassion; critique credulity and social hostility that target vulnerable people (the 'Moll White' example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of confidants who proxy for others
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidents (attainders' attendants) 'assume to themselves the Merit of the Persons whom they have in their Custody' and are 'of all People the most impertinent.' They can govern who may approach and how courtship is conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying social interactions, mark the presence and influence of confidants; as advice, 'set a Mark upon Confidents' — they often complicate relations and may misrepresent or control access. Use them as social-observational devices in essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-breeding: favour naturalness and ease over ceremony
rubrics_metrics.description: An unconstrained carriage and a certain Openness of Behaviour are 'the Height of Good Breeding.' The 'Modish World' has thrown off superfluous deference and ceremony in favour of agreeable negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writing about manners (and in stylistic practice), prefer naturalness and ease to ostentatious forms. Good manners should appear subtle and unforced: 'Good Breeding shews it self most, where to an ordinary Eye it appears the least.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggerated politeness that betrays inexperience
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive ceremonial manners (many bows, over-attention to precedence) indicate that one has not conversed much in the world; a polite country squire may make as many bows in half an hour 'as would serve a Courtier for a Week.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique and avoid theatrical or overelaborate civility in characters or conduct; let true politeness be unshowy. In composition, don't over-ornament prose to signal refinement — excessive artifice reads as inauthentic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against coarseness in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where once obscene ideas were clothed in modest terms, contemporary conversation has relapsed so that 'several of our Men of the Town... make use of the most coarse uncivilized Words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a normative standard, maintain modest phrasing for vulgar topics; avoid adopting fashionable coarseness which the author treats as a decline in good manners. This is both a social and stylistic injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural observation to support philosophical arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for Providence drawn from the natural history of animals are called 'demonstrative' — e.g., the specific structure of animals suits their ways of life and parental care patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground abstract or theological claims in concrete, observable instances from nature (nests, parental behaviour, instinct). Employ carefully chosen natural examples (the hen and her nest, the bitch and her puppy) to illustrate and persuade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise limits of human reason when explaining instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues that many animal behaviours 'cannot be Imitation' nor 'Reason' — instinct shows sagacity in narrow particulars but lacks the generality of human reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining non-human behaviour, avoid anthropomorphizing or assuming full rational agency; instead, use analogical reasoning cautiously and acknowledge mystery or limits (invoking instinct or divine impression when appropriate).
